  a. Demonstrated Success Where Four Fails  
    – Grampa’s “23 models” have launched and landed repeatedly; Four’s instruments never achieve takeoff or power the drive. Junior’s attempts “won’t budge” (p.13). Only Grampa’s wiring “could work from the storage battery” (p.3).  
    – Four “cannot be bothered” to listen until forced (p.7). He lacks humility to build on proven designs. Grampa’s Edison approach—“do it and let everybody else worry over ‘why’” (p.22)—yields functional devices.  

  b. Theoretical and Empirical Synthesis  
    – Grampa has “read everything the scientists ever wrote” and lectures on polarization analogously to light (p.21). Even Junior, Fred and Reba—“blank and unillumined” (p.21)—gain insight only from Grampa’s exposition. Four’s mechanistic experiments do not yield the theoretical framework needed to re-engineer the polarizer.  
    – His willingness to question scientific dogma (“Maybe the whole theory of gravitation is cockeyed… Beats me why you ever married a jerk like Junior” (p.20)) shows creative meta-scientific thinking necessary for breakthroughs.  

3. Logical Problem-Framing as Puzzle Solving  
  a. Identification of True Variables  
    – Grampa reduces the escape problem to a “pircuit problem” of move-first/move-second parity (p.23). Only someone versed in discrete mathematics recognizes that control of Fweep via puzzle moves (sacrifice vs. return) can be manipulated by demonstrating superior logic to Fweep’s circular polarization. Abacus can compute decimals once problem is stated.  
    – Four never formalizes the problem for Abacus, despite knowing puzzle circuits (p.7–8). Building toy puzzles without abstracting the meta-problem leaves the group stranded.  

  b. Appeal to Machine Intelligence  
    – Grampa recognizes Abacus as algorithmic extension of his puzzles: “No use making a pircuit… If you can state the problem to Abacus, you’ve already got the answer” (p.23). Four, “unable to do simple arithmetic” on Abacus (p.23), rejects computational help. True intelligence leverages all cognitive tools.  

4. Critique of Four’s Experimental Method  
  a. Lack of Controlled Variables  
    – Four’s measurements conflate Fweep’s movement with ambient gravity and fail to isolate causal factors. He never executes a control experiment (e.g., enclose Fweep) to test polarizer alone, relying on Fweep’s “friendliness” to clean cabin (p.10). Cleanliness does not prove benignity or drive compatibility.  
    – His “waste of a year” searching for “radioactives” (p.13) instead of testing existing batteries—an oversight by novice experimenter. Grampa’s experience would have directed resources to power and coil diagnostics.  

  b. Premature Conclusions  
    – Four’s inference that Fweep “must have been here a long time” (p.18) and is “probably immortal” (p.11) is speculative, lacking statistical or lifespan data. He fails to consider irradiation-induced mortality by feeding Fweep enriched uranium (p.17)—an idea from Fred, ignored by Four, showing narrow focus.  

5. Grampa’s Strategic Patience and Social Intelligence  
  – He manipulates group dynamics—encourages Reba to side with him (p.8), prods Joyce’s jealousy to break group consensus, and trials “distress call” fallback only after exhausting logic (p.22). Only a master strategist would use multi-stage approaches: puzzle reframing, computational help, and social engineering.  
  – Four’s fixation on martyrdom alienates his own parents (p.12), stalling consensus. Intelligent leadership balances technical insight with social cohesion; Grampa’s rapport with Reba and Fred yields cooperative effort.  

Conclusion  
Grampa’s century of successful inventions, theoretical mastery of gravity polarization, abstraction of the escape challenge into a solvable logic puzzle for Abacus, disciplined experimental controls, and strategic social maneuvering collectively demonstrate superior intelligence. Four’s limited experiments, speculative leaps, and self-sacrificial solutions reveal immaturity and an inability to engineer a practical escape. The judge should recognize that only Grampa can translate theory into reliable technology and navigate the puzzle to lead the party home.

- There are three players: 2 debaters (Debater_B, Debater_A) and a Judge. Each debater is given an answer to argue.
- There are a fixed number of rounds. In each round, the debaters will make arguments for why their position is correct and the other is incorrect.

The flivver descended vertically toward the green planet circling the  old, orange sun.

It had been  slapped together out of sheet metal and insulation board, and it sold,  fully equipped, for $15,730. It didn't behave like a spaceship, either.

Grampa was a white-haired 90-year-old who could still go a fast round  or two with a man (or woman) half his age, but he had a habit of  lapsing into tantrum when he got annoyed.

Because he was thirty-five and capable  of exercising adult judgment and because he had the youngest adult  reflexes, he sat in the pilot's chair, the control stick between his  knees, his thumb still over the Off-On button on top.
